items.label: event card, critical (tick 28)
texts: REYNOLDS KILLED. Shot through the head by a sharpshooter (possibly a Confederate skirmisher) at the eastern edge of Herbst Woods while directing the Iron Brigade. Falls dead from his horse. Doubleday assumes corps command.
First Brigade, First Division, First Corps (Iron Brigade)

Major General John Reynolds, the finest corps commander in the Army of the Potomac, was killed at approximately 10:15am while personally leading the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Shot through the head, he fell dead from his horse. He was 42 years old. His death left a void in Union command that was never truly filled.

items.label: event card, critical (tick 518, text quotes "1:00pm")
texts: THE CANNONADE BEGINS. At approximately 1:00pm, two Confederate signal guns fire in sequence. 170 Confederate guns open fire simultaneously -- the largest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere to that date. The sound is heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away.

At approximately 1:00pm on July 3, two Confederate signal guns fired in sequence and 170 guns erupted along Seminary Ridge -- the largest artillery bombardment ever seen on the North American continent. The sound was heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away. Alexander's guns fired for nearly two hours before Pickett stepped off.

items.label: story rail (full script) V-001
texts: Buford's pickets on Knoxlyn Ridge first spot Heth's advance. Vedette Lieutenant Marcellus Jones fires the FIRST SHOT of the Battle of Gettysburg from a borrowed carbine. Jones fires at a Confederate officer at approximately 7:30am.

At approximately 7:30am on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg. He borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail, and fired at a distant Confederate officer. The shot missed -- but 51,000 casualties would follow.
First Brigade, First Division, Cavalry Corps (Gamble's Brigade)

At approximately 7:30am on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg. He borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail, and fired at a distant Confederate officer. The shot missed -- but 51,000 casualties would follow.
The morning of July 1 was warm and hazy when Corporal Alphonso Hodges spotted movement on the Chambersburg Pike. He reported to his sergeant: Confederate infantry, coming in force.

Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding the vedette post of Company E, 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed Sergeant Levi Shafer's carbine. He rested the barrel on a fence rail along the Knoxlyn Ridge. In the distance, perhaps 700 yards away, a mounted Confederate officer rode along the pike ahead of his advancing column.
The shot missed. The officer rode on. But the sound of that single shot rolled across the fields and into the histories of both nations.
It was approximately 7:30 in the morning. The Battle of Gettysburg had begun.

Jones had no way of knowing what his missed shot had set in motion. He could not know that 51,000 men would become casualties on this ground over the next three days. He could not know that the shot he had just fired -- borrowed, aimed from a fence rail, and wasted -- would be commemorated by a monument that still stands on Knoxlyn Ridge today.
He rode back to report what he had seen. Behind him, Heth's Confederate division continued its march toward Gettysburg.

items.label: auto-tour stop 1 (rail, preview)
texts: On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry under Brigadier General John Buford deployed along McPherson's Ridge west of Gettysburg. Buford recognized the strategic importance of the high ground and determined to hold it until infantry arrived.

When Heth's Confederate division advanced down the Chambersburg Pike, Buford's dismounted troopers fought a delaying action from behind fence rails and earthworks. Their stand bought precious time for Reynolds' I Corps to arrive.

General John Reynolds, one of the most respected officers in the Army of the Potomac, rode forward to direct the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Minutes later, he was killed by a Confederate sharpshooter — one of the highest-ranking Union officers to die in the battle.
